newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Air pocket saves Australian landslide victim.
newsitem.headline: Air pocket saves Australian landslide victim.

text.p: A massive concrete slab, a pocket of air and freezing alpine temperatures have ironically combined to protect a man buried alive for more than 60 hours under the ruins of two Australian ski lodges engulfed by a landslide.
The concrete slab which entombed the man, not only prevented him from being crushed, but also created an air pocket insulating him from plummeting overnight temperatures.
Temperatures fell to around minus 12 degrees Celsius (10 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, freezing the water-cooled diamond drills being used by rescuers to break-up concrete slabs.
Ironically, the cold helped boost the survival chances of the man, identified by local media as ski instructor Stuart Diver, by slowing down his metabolism, said medical experts.
"Miracles do happen," Australian Medical Association spokesman Keith Woollard said on Saturday.
"We have our lines of time that we believe people can survive under extreme circumstances but every now and then somebody manages to do something which is absolutely remarkable," Woolard said.

"His condition is likely to be pretty miserable obviously and there's no knowing what injuries he might have sustained. The fact that he has managed to survive these conditions is probably a tribute to his own personal strength," he said.
Dr John Vinen, the head of emergency medicine at Sydney's Royal North Shore Hospital, said the air pocket in which the man is trapped had probably insulated him from the cold.
"Presumably if he's survived this long he can't be too badly injured," Vinen told Reuters.
The man has told rescuers that he has little feeling in his body, but is able to move in the cramped conditions.

Vinen said the man's lack of feeling was probably a result of hypothermia, or having been crushed by debris. "The first thing they'll have to do when they get him out is test he's core body temperature and test for crush syndrome," he said.
Crush syndrome is caused by being trapped in a confined space which compresses muscles, resulting in decreased blood supply, which can release toxins into the bloodstream and lead to kidney failure.
The landslide hit just before midnight on Wednesday at Australia's most popular ski resort, the Thredbo Alpine Village in the Snowy Mountains, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.

Tonnes of soil, rock and gum trees crushed the Carinya lodge, sending it cascading onto the Bimbadeen lodge. Nineteen people were buried in the lodges, while a woman walking home with her husband was swept away with the landslide.
Rescuers have confirmed three deaths but only one body has been recovered.
After virtually giving up hope of finding survivors among the 20 people trapped under the rubble, rescuers heard a muffled voice on Saturday morning.

Vinen said people were resilient and provided they were not badly injured, could survive for up to 10 days without food and that someone had survived four days in hypothermic conditions after being trapped by an avalanche in North America.
He said the trapped Thredbo man may have been able to get water from condensation or snow -- vital for his survival.

Recent disasters have produced some triumphs of human survival. In the Mexico earthquake in 1985, 20 survivors were found after eight days, while in 1991, after one of China's worst recorded earthquakes, a woman was pulled alive from the ruins after surviving for 13 days.
